entry.title: [@sveltejs/kit] SvelteKit : XSS via untrusted cache-control header in prerendered page
entry.content:
Impact

Applications that prerender pages and use setHeaders to set a cache-control header from an untrusted source are vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS).

SvelteKit inserts the header value into a <meta http-equiv="cache-control"> tag without escaping it. An attacker who can influence this value at prerender time can break out of the content attribute and inject HTML or JavaScript into the generated page. The injected code can then execute when users visit the page.

Patches

The fix escapes the header value before inserting it into the generated HTML. Upgrade to @sveltejs/kit version 3.0.0 or later.

Workarounds

Avoid forwarding untrusted cache-control header values with setHeaders on prerendered pages. Use a fixed, trusted cache policy instead.

References

  • https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/security/advisories/GHSA-27mw-82g8-phjj
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114061
  • https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/commit/d9d55b579743c80ee7cb59c272d864fd9253dae7
  • https://github.com/sveltejs/kit/releases/tag/@sveltejs/kit@3.0.0
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/sveltekit-before-3.0.0-xss-via-cache-control-header-in-prerendered-pages
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-27mw-82g8-phjj

entry.title: [@sveltejs/kit] Duplicate Advisory: SvelteKit before 3.0.0 XSS via Cache-Control Header in Prerendered Pages
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-27mw-82g8-phjj. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

SvelteKit (@sveltejs/kit) before 3.0.0 contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability in prerendered pages because a cache-control header value set via setHeaders is inserted without escaping into a tag. An attacker who can influence that untrusted value at prerender time can break out of the content attribute and inject HTML or JavaScript that executes when users visit the page.

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc: Memory-lifecycle tools overwrite unowned notes or partially commit lifecycle changes
entry.content:
Summary

create_entity, link_entities, rename_entity, unlink_entities and delete_entity regenerate a memory note's body from SQLite at the computed memory/<type>/<name>.md path. When a note already existed at that path and was not owned by the entity being written (a hand-authored note, or an orphan left by a different entity whose name sanitized to the same path), its entire body was overwritten on the next write naming that (type, name), keeping only its frontmatter. Separately, several of these tools inserted or removed their SQLite row before the fallible filesystem step, so a refused note write could leave a relation gone, a retired status committed, or the wrong entity deleted.

Details

  • create_entity and link_entities inserted the SQL row or relation before materialization.
  • rename_entity seeded the destination path with a direct atomic write that bypassed the ownership check, and for a status-only rename could commit a retired status with the note write refused.
  • unlink_entities removed the relation row before discovering the source note's rematerialization would be refused.
  • delete_entity's cascade could delete the target and its relations before a neighbour's note was found to be foreign.

The overwrite exists in every released version since materializeEntity shipped (git show v1.0.1:packages/server/src/memory/materialize.ts).

Impact

An authorized caller with memory-write scope (any agent using the M5 memory tools) can, without intending to, destroy the body of a vault note outside the entity it is writing, and can leave the memory graph inconsistent with the notes on disk. Snapshots-before-write (restore_note) mitigate the overwrite only where snapshots are enabled and the note had been written through obsidian-tc before.

Patches

Fixed in 1.31.4 at the shared primitive: materializeEntity refuses to write over a note whose obsidian_tc_id is missing or belongs to another entity; a new assertNoteOwnership pre-check runs before any SQLite mutation in the three lifecycle tools, so a refusal is a no-op; create_entity and link_entities roll back the row they had inserted. Verified by test/m5-memory-ownership.test.ts, which covers all five call sites and the rollback.

Workarounds

None that preserve the tools. Disabling the write:memory scope for callers prevents the write path entirely.

Credit

Found by the maintainer while building obsidian-tc memory import (PR #978); the vulnerability class was independently confirmed by a cross-vendor adversarial review.

References

  • PR #978 (fix and test), CHANGELOG ## [1.31.4] ### Security
  • packages/server/src/memory/materialize.ts, packages/server/src/tools/m5/memory-lifecycle-tools.ts

References

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc HTTP transport lacks Origin/DNS-rebinding protection, enabling drive-by vault access on loopback
entry.content:
Impact

The Streamable HTTP transport was constructed without enableDnsRebindingProtection/allowedHosts/allowedOrigins and performed no Origin-header validation. With the documented auth.mode: "none" loopback default, a drive-by web page could POST http://127.0.0.1/mcp and receive caller http-local with scopes ["*"] — full vault read/write — via DNS rebinding / a forged Origin.

Patches

Fixed in 1.3.1. Upgrade to >= 1.3.1. The transport now enables DNS-rebinding protection and allowed hosts/origins and returns HTTP 403 on an invalid Origin (per MCP 2025-11-25).

Workarounds

Do not expose the HTTP transport with auth.mode: "none"; require JWT auth, or bind to a non-loopback interface behind a proxy that validates Origin.

References

  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/security/advisories/GHSA-pqh8-4pj7-32xx
  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/pull/74
  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/commit/6428bfe6fdfd43aa7b4b369be3aecd6a268fb928

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc Bridge tools leak denied-note data via unfiltered sibling fields
entry.content:
Impact

Bridge tool results filtered only the items array against the read ACL and passed sibling fields through unfiltered: tasks_filter emitted groups whose counts reflected denied notes, makemd_query returned ...result siblings, and list_templates enumerated Templater template paths and parsed user-function bodies with no read-whitelist gate. A caller could infer or read data from notes outside its read ACL.

Patches

Fixed in 1.3.1. Upgrade to >= 1.3.1. All path-attributable fields are now scrubbed or fail-closed, and list_templates is gated on the read whitelist.

Workarounds

Disable the affected bridge tools (tasks_filter, makemd_query, list_templates) via tool visibility.

References

  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/security/advisories/GHSA-43r2-c7g8-prc8

entry.title: [zod] Zod can exhaust memory while validating oversized constrained collections
entry.content:
Zod schema-validation library through 4.6.5 contains an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability that allows attackers to exhaust memory by submitting a large array to an application using an array schema without a length constraint. Attackers can exploit the handleArrayResult parse logic in $ZodArray, which accumulates every validation issue for each failing element with no cap or early termination, causing the process to allocate excessive issue objects and crash due to out-of-memory conditions.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-54404
  • https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/1872

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc: Declined human-in-the-loop confirmations can permit destructive calls over HTTP
entry.content:
Summary

On a Streamable HTTP deployment with auth.jwtSecret configured, serving a 2026-07-28-era client that declared elicitation.form support, a call to a dispatch-gated tool (destructive: true, or a scope with an HITL floor) that was offered an inputRequired confirmation could still complete after the human declined, cancelled, or the elicitation response was omitted or malformed, provided the client echoed the validly bound requestState on resubmission. The server trusted an authentic, call-bound state as proof of approval; the state is minted before the elicitation leg is asked, so it proves only that the resubmission belongs to the same call.

Details

Reproduced directly: a destructive: true tool call, offered inputRequired, answered with {action: "decline"} on the elicitation/create leg, still wrote. Present since the 2026-07-28 round trip shipped in v1.13.0 (THE-583). Only dispatch-gated tools were reachable; the sixteen handler-side conditionally gated tools (write_note overwrite, move_note, and others) did not read the elicitation state on the modern wire at all, so they neither let a decline nor an approval through.

Impact

A client that echoes state after a decline can execute destructive vault operations (delete, cross-folder move, frontmatter replace, link rewrite) that the human explicitly refused. The precondition is a compliant client behaving incorrectly or a client under an attacker's control; the human's refusal is not enforced by the server.

Patches

Fixed in 1.31.4: the server now also requires the confirm leg's own response (inputResponse) to be {action: "accept", content: {approve: true}} before trusting the echoed state. A declined, cancelled or not-approved round renders the ordinary elicit_required error and is never offered a second round for the same declined confirmation. The same release adds server-initiated in-band confirmation on stdio (legacy era), so stdio agents no longer need to mint elicit_token themselves.

Not addressed

A malicious or non-compliant client can still answer its own elicitation/create leg with an approval regardless of what the human said. The server cannot verify that the client rendered the form or that a human saw it; this is inherent to the client-driven half of the 2026-07-28 protocol. The legacy shim, where the server sends and owns the leg, does not share this gap.

Workarounds

Run affected deployments over stdio, or leave auth.jwtSecret unset so the requestState codec (and therefore inputRequired) is never offered; both fall back to the CLI elicit_token path.

Credit

Reported in GH #967; found and closed under THE-1106 (PR #969); the residual is documented in SECURITY.md.

References

  • PR #969, GH #967, CHANGELOG ## [1.31.4] ### Security
  • packages/server/src/mcp/server.ts (tools/call handler), packages/server/src/vault/hitl.ts

References

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc tokens can access arbitrary configured vaults
entry.content:
Impact

Tool dispatch did not check the caller-supplied input.vault against the caller's bound vault (ctx.vaultId); the folder ACL was a single global instance and the JWT carried no vault claim. As a result, any valid token could read, write, or delete any configured vault by passing input.vault, defeating multi-tenant isolation across ~90 tool sites. (resources/read was the only surface that already guarded this.)

Patches

Fixed in 1.3.1 (the fix was developed on the v1.3.0 tag, which never published to npm; 1.3.1 is the first published release with the fix). Upgrade to >= 1.3.1.

Workarounds

Run a single vault per server process, or isolate each tenant on a separate process/credential.

Fix

A central input.vault === ctx.vaultId guard was added in dispatch before the scope check.

References

  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/security/advisories/GHSA-84c9-qqpq-2pq5
  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/pull/72

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-77366

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc: Default folder ACL is fail-open; .obsidian plugin secrets are readable by default
entry.content:
Impact

With a default configuration, an undefined readPaths/writePaths meant allow-all, the strictReadDefault flag was inert, and the .obsidian/.git/.trash control directories were denied only during enumeration — not on the direct request path. A caller could read .obsidian/plugins/*/data.json, exfiltrating plugin API keys and Obsidian Sync passwords (live-reproduced), as well as any other in-vault file by path.

Patches

Fixed in 1.3.1. Upgrade to >= 1.3.1. The default now denies .obsidian/.git/.trash on read/write/delete and honors strictReadDefault on the request path.

Workarounds

Set an explicit readPaths/writePaths whitelist that excludes the control directories.

References

  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/security/advisories/GHSA-cvp8-vvgf-69q4
  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/pull/73

entry.title: [obsidian-tc] obsidian-tc : Symlink read-ACL scope bypass via lexical path checks
entry.content:
Impact

ACL checks ran on the lexical vault-relative path while containment used the realpath. An in-vault symlink placed under an allowed glob, whose realpath resolved into a denied folder, passed the read ACL — an intra-vault read-ACL-scope bypass. It requires an out-of-band-planted symlink (no MCP tool creates one) and is not a vault-root escape.

Patches

Fixed in 1.3.1. Upgrade to >= 1.3.1. ACL enforcement now derives the realpath vault-relative path and feeds a single unified predicate at every site.

Workarounds

Do not permit untrusted symlinks inside the vault.

References

  • https://github.com/The-40-Thieves/obsidian-tc/security/advisories/GHSA-c5xx-h28h-f682

entry.title: [@nuxt/nitro-server] Nuxt: Server-side route rules (`redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr`) are skipped for case-variant paths when routing is case-insensitive
entry.content:
Impact

With the default router.options.sensitive: false, Nuxt's page router resolves routes case-insensitively, so /Admin renders the same page as /admin. On the server, however, route rules were resolved with Nitro's route-rule matcher, which matches keys case-sensitively. A request whose path differs from a rule key only in letter case therefore rendered the page with none of that rule applied.

Earlier fixes (GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47, GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9) case-folded the route rules that the Nuxt app itself reads, such as appMiddleware. This advisory covers the rules applied on the server:

  • redirect: a rule used to send visitors away from a page, such as '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }, was skipped, and the page and its server-fetched data were rendered instead.
  • headers: per-route response headers, including security headers such as Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options, were not sent.
  • proxy: the request was not proxied.
  • ssr: false and noScripts: the page was server-rendered, or shipped scripts, despite the rule.
  • getRouteRules(event) (auto-imported, or from nuxt/server) and matchRouteRules from nuxt/server returned no rules for the case variant.
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})

With this configuration, /admin/secret redirects to /login, but /Admin/secret rendered app/pages/admin/secret.vue.

Mitigating factors

  • Applications that set router.options.sensitive: true in nuxt.config are not affected, because their pages are only served for the exact case of the route.
  • Access checks performed in server middleware, route middleware attached with definePageMeta, or in the page's data fetching are not affected. The issue only affects protections that rely on a server-side route rule matching the request path.

Affected versions

nuxt <4.6.2, including all Nuxt 3 releases, and @nuxt/nitro-server <4.6.2.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt@4.6.2. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Nuxt now resolves server-side route rules itself, decoding and case-folding both the rule keys and the request path unless router.options.sensitive is set, and applies the result to Nitro's redirect, headers and proxy handling, the renderer, and the getRouteRules / matchRouteRules helpers.

When routing is case-insensitive, patched releases change some behaviour:

  • Route rules also apply to case variants of server API routes. For example, /API/x now matches a /api/** proxy or headers rule.
  • Rule keys that differ only in letter case now resolve to the same path on the server, and the later key takes precedence.

The following are not changed by this fix:

  • cache and swr response caching is attached to server routes by Nitro's router, which matches case-sensitively. A case variant is still rendered with its route rules applied, but its response is not cached.
  • Rules that a deployment preset compiles into platform configuration (for example Vercel's config.json or Netlify's _redirects and _headers) are matched by the platform. Once a request reaches the Nuxt server, the rules are applied as described above.
  • If sensitive is set only in app/router.options.ts, the server follows the nuxt.config value. In that configuration route rules can only apply to more paths, never fewer.

Workarounds

Upgrade to nuxt@4.6.2. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

  1. Set router: { options: { sensitive: true } } in nuxt.config, so pages are only served for the exact case of their route.
  2. Alternatively, enforce access control in server middleware or route middleware rather than relying on a redirect route rule, and set security headers for every response rather than per route.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-vjh5-4x84-xrqp
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114132
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/f6cfee52cf9576ddc4f4ee83b486969328b358f8
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/releases/tag/v4.6.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vjh5-4x84-xrqp

  • Route rules also apply to case variants of server API routes. For example, /API/x now matches a /api/** proxy or headers rule.

  • cache and swr response caching is attached to server routes by Nitro's router, which matches case-sensitively. A case variant is still rendered with its route rules applied, but its response is not cached.

Upgrade to nuxt@4.6.2. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

  1. Set router: { options: { sensitive: true } } in nuxt.config, so pages are only served for the exact case of their route.

entry.title: [nuxt] Nuxt: Server-side route rules (`redirect`, `headers`, `proxy`, `ssr`) are skipped for case-variant paths when routing is case-insensitive
entry.content:
Impact

With the default router.options.sensitive: false, Nuxt's page router resolves routes case-insensitively, so /Admin renders the same page as /admin. On the server, however, route rules were resolved with Nitro's route-rule matcher, which matches keys case-sensitively. A request whose path differs from a rule key only in letter case therefore rendered the page with none of that rule applied.

Earlier fixes (GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47, GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9) case-folded the route rules that the Nuxt app itself reads, such as appMiddleware. This advisory covers the rules applied on the server:

  • redirect: a rule used to send visitors away from a page, such as '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }, was skipped, and the page and its server-fetched data were rendered instead.
  • headers: per-route response headers, including security headers such as Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options, were not sent.
  • proxy: the request was not proxied.
  • ssr: false and noScripts: the page was server-rendered, or shipped scripts, despite the rule.
  • getRouteRules(event) (auto-imported, or from nuxt/server) and matchRouteRules from nuxt/server returned no rules for the case variant.
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' },
  },
})

entry.title: [nuxt] Nuxt server islands render `useHeadSafe` input without sanitisation
entry.content:
Impact

useHeadSafe restricts head input to an allowlist of safe tags and attributes. For example, bodyAttrs is limited to class and style, event handler attributes are removed, and <script> tags are only kept for JSON types.

When useHeadSafe is called inside a server island (a .server.vue component or page, or a component rendered with <NuxtIsland>), the island renderer serialises the raw input of every head entry into the island response without the option that marks it as safe input. <NuxtIsland> then pushes that input into the page's head as a regular entry, both during server rendering and when hydrating or refetching on the client.

As a result, input that useHeadSafe would normally strip (such as bodyAttrs.onload or executable <script> content) is rendered into the page. If an application passes user-controlled data to useHeadSafe inside a server island, an attacker who controls that data can achieve stored cross-site scripting on the application's origin.

<!-- components/AuthorMeta.server.vue -->
<script setup lang="ts">
const { data: author } = await useFetch('/api/author')
// author.value.head is user-authored, e.g. { bodyAttrs: { onload: '...' } }
useHeadSafe(author.value.head)
</script>

Mitigating factors

  • Server components are experimental. They are only active when the application defines a .server.vue component or page, or enables experimental.componentIslands and renders <NuxtIsland>.
  • Exploitation requires the application to pass attacker-controlled data to useHeadSafe inside a server island. useHeadSafe called from regular (non-island) components and pages is not affected.

Affected versions

nuxt >=3.13.0, when head support for server islands was introduced. Nuxt 2 is not affected.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt@4.6.2. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Patched releases apply Unhead's safe input filtering to useHeadSafe entries on the server before they are added to the island response, so islandResponse.head (including what render:island hooks see) only contains input that useHeadSafe allows.

Workarounds

Upgrade to nuxt@4.6.2. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3:

  1. Call useHeadSafe with untrusted input from a regular component or page rather than from inside a server island.
  2. Alternatively, validate untrusted head input against your own allowlist before passing it to useHeadSafe inside a server island.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-xfq5-w38q-pc2x
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114133
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/493565e99451a0f52330b1f6b979254a4a39e5d0
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/releases/tag/v4.6.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xfq5-w38q-pc2x

entry.title: [nuxt] Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26: a `javascript:` URL prefixed with an ASCII control character executes from `<NuxtLink>` when `pages` is disabled
entry.content:
Impact

An application that renders <NuxtLink :to="..."> with a value it does not control can be made to render an anchor whose href executes script in the application's origin when clicked.

This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26 (CVE-2026-53722). It only affects applications running without a pages/ directory, where pages resolves to false and Nuxt registers its own router in place of vue-router. Applications using vue-router are not affected.

Prefixing javascript: with an ASCII C0 control character, for example %01, meant the value was not recognised as having a protocol. It was classified as an internal route and so never reached the protocol check added in GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26, and the router used for pages: false passed it through to the rendered href unchanged. Browsers strip the leading control character and run the result as a script URL.

Both <NuxtLink custom> and the default anchor are affected, and the href is present in the server-rendered HTML.

Mitigating factors

  • The application must have pages disabled (no pages/ directory, or pages: false).
  • The application must bind untrusted input to :to.
  • A victim must click the rendered link.

Affected versions

nuxt <4.6.0, including all Nuxt 3 releases. Versions before 4.4.7 and 3.21.7 are also affected by GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt@4.6.0. Nuxt 3 reached end of life on 31 July 2026 and will not receive a fix.

Anchor href values are now checked for script-capable protocols wherever they are rendered, including the router used when pages is disabled. Protocol detection also moved to the platform URL parser, so a URL is classified the same way the browser will read it.

Workarounds

Upgrade to nuxt@4.6.0 or later. If you cannot upgrade, including on Nuxt 3, validate values before binding them to :to, for example by rejecting anything that is not a path beginning with a single /.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-jjm6-p2m9-9w4x
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114130

entry.title: [nuxt] Nuxt: Route rules are matched against the raw request path, so a percent-encoded segment can bypass `appMiddleware` on dynamic and catch-all routes
entry.content:
Summary

Nuxt compared routeRules keys against the raw request path, without decoding percent-encoding, while the router decodes parameters when it resolves a route. A request whose path is percent-encoded can therefore resolve to a page while failing to match the route rule meant to protect it, so the rule's appMiddleware never runs, including during server rendering.

Impact

For a page served through a dynamic or catch-all route, an attacker can percent-encode a character in the path to skip the rule:

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/users/admin': { appMiddleware: 'auth' },
  },
})

Requesting /users/%61dmin still renders app/pages/users/[id].vue with id decoded to admin, but the rule keyed /users/admin does not match, so auth does not run and the server renders and returns the gated page to an unauthenticated visitor. No privileges and no user interaction are required, and only ASCII characters are involved.

Purely static ASCII routes are not affected: static segments are matched without decoding, so a request for /%61dmin does not resolve to the page registered at /admin and 404s instead of rendering.

The rule keys affected are the ones carried in the app manifest and consumed by the app: appMiddleware, redirect, appLayout, ssr, prerender, and the payload flags derived from cache, isr and swr.

If you have pinned or overridden dependency versions below what your Nuxt release declares, a release outside the affected ranges can still be exposed, so do not conclude from a single reproduction that you are unaffected.

Patches

Releases from 4.4.4 and 3.21.4 are not affected, because their dependency floor requires a version of the underlying HTTP layer that normalises percent-encoding in the request path before routing, which removes the mismatch in a default install.

The comparison itself is fixed in nuxt@4.5.2 and nuxt@3.21.11: route-rule keys and lookup paths are now decoded (and, unless router.options.sensitive is set, case-folded) before they are compared. Reserved escapes such as %2F are left encoded, so decoding cannot introduce extra path segments, and paths that cannot be decoded are matched verbatim. Upgrading to those releases is recommended, since it fixes the comparison rather than relying on a dependency to normalise the input, and it also restores route rules for pages whose paths contain non-ASCII characters.

Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, do not rely on a routeRules key alone to protect a route. Attach the middleware to the page itself, which binds it to the resolved route rather than to the raw path string:

<script setup lang="ts">
definePageMeta({ middleware: 'auth' })
</script>

Credits

Thanks to @sushi-gif, whose report that route rules keyed with non-ASCII paths never match the routes generated for those pages prompted the review that found this issue.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-6gq8-jgmh-3ffp
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114131
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/81f86ac5ee82bb1a9b887e59f3bc84624d711497
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/9123ed850c468a7424a868c20d0d49a5507d32e5

entry.title: [electron] Electron: SameSite cookie restrictions are not applied to windows opened from links
entry.content:
Impact

Pages opened into a new window from a link were loaded as if the app itself had navigated there rather than the page that contained the link, so the request was treated as same-site: SameSite=Strict cookies were sent and Sec-Fetch-Site did not identify the initiating page. Content shown in the app could use this to make a credentialed top-level request to another site that relies on SameSite cookies as a CSRF defence.

Apps are only affected if they load untrusted content and allow it to open new windows. Apps that deny new windows from untrusted content with setWindowOpenHandler are not affected.

Workarounds

Return { action: 'deny' } from setWindowOpenHandler for windows opened by untrusted content.

Fixed Versions

  • 45.0.0-alpha.6
  • 44.3.0
  • 43.7.0
  • 42.11.3

For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at security@electronjs.org
